items.text: You're not bad at resting. Masking doesn't pause when you take a break. Autistic burnout recovery needs reduced demands, not just downtime.
items.rationale: Leads with the self-blame readers already carry, then redirects it to the structural mismatch — lands as relief, not lecture. Directly contradicts 'just take a break' advice without dismissing the advice-giver.

items.text: The problem with 'just rest' advice for autistic burnout: the thing draining you — masking — doesn't stop while you sleep.
items.rationale: Tight single-sentence reframe that names the mechanism. Quotable and screenshot-able — exactly the kind of post someone sends to a partner who keeps suggesting 'a holiday would help'.

items.text: 'Won't' is a moral judgment. 'Can't' is information. For PDAers, demand avoidance is a threat response — the nervous system is braking, not the person.
items.rationale: The two-sentence opener does the heavy lifting before the explanation lands. 'Braking, not the person' keeps the block with the nervous system, not character — shifts the frame without excusing or minimising.

items.text: Late autism diagnosis doesn't just bring relief. There's grief too — for the decades spent building an identity around masking. Mourning who you had to be is real.
items.rationale: Names a specific, under-articulated grief without collapsing it into relief or anger. 'Mourning who you had to be' gives the feeling a precise container. No pity, no silver lining forced in.

items.text: ADHD content felt close but not quite. Autistic content did too. If neither box ever fully fit, that's not you failing to fit — that's the boxes.
items.rationale: Speaks directly to the pre-AuDHD-identification experience without using the label as a punchline or a sales pitch. Affirms without performing positivity.

items.text: Which community finally felt like home — ADHD spaces, autistic spaces, or neither until AuDHD clicked? Curious what the turning point was.
items.rationale: Invites lived-experience sharing without leading the witness. 'Curious what the turning point was' signals genuine interest, not engagement farming. Should surface a wide range of stories.

items.text: Remote work wasn't a perk for a lot of autistic and ADHD people. It was an accommodation. Calling it back without alternatives isn't a culture question — it's an access one.
items.rationale: Timely given live RTO policy news. Shifts the frame from preference/laziness to disability access without being preachy. 'A lot of' avoids universalising. Likely the post with the most reach this week.

items.text: Does 'Persistent Drive for Autonomy' feel more accurate to you — or does removing 'pathological' erase how disabling it can actually be?
items.rationale: Genuine open question with no clean answer — rare on social media. Holds both sides honestly without steering toward either. Should draw thoughtful replies from across the PDA community spectrum.

items.text: 68% of neurodivergent workers don't know what accommodations they can ask for. Not because they don't exist — because nobody told them. Know your options before the next hard conversation at work.
items.rationale: Concrete stat, concrete takeaway, no moralising. 'Nobody told them' rather than 'employers won't give them' makes the problem feel solvable rather than just bleak. Good anchor for a follow-up list post.
items.sensitivity_flag: Stat drawn from a 2025 Neurodiversity at Work survey cited in the briefing — confirm exact survey name and public attributability before posting.

items.text: Autistic burnout doesn't usually hit when life gets busy. It hits at transitions — new job, university, parenthood — when the scaffolding disappears and you have to rebuild everything at once.
items.rationale: Answers the unasked question 'why did I fall apart at 23/38/45 when I'd coped fine before?' Reframes burnout timing from personal failure to a predictable systems pattern. Specific examples make it recognisable fast.

items.text: Low-demand parenting isn't giving up on structure. It's reducing the neurological alarm that makes any cooperation impossible. You can't reach a nervous system in threat mode.
items.rationale: Addresses the central shame point for PDA parents — being seen as permissive — and replaces it with a mechanistic explanation. 'You can't reach a nervous system in threat mode' is blunt and memorable enough to repeat to sceptical relatives.

items.text: AuDHD burnout recovery needs enough novelty to engage the ADHD brain and enough predictability to settle the autistic nervous system. Those pull in opposite directions. Most recovery advice picks one.
items.rationale: Names a genuine internal contradiction that neither ADHD-only nor autistic-only content captures. The last sentence does the work — it's the thing people forward to partners and therapists who keep suggesting advice that only half-fits.
